structure.title: The Window · Tomorrow's weather
structure.text: James Ramsay is cutting pictures out of a catalogue when his mother tells him they might sail to the lighthouse tomorrow. His father predicts rain. To James this is an act of cruelty. Woolf spends the afternoon and evening moving between people for whom the very same words have meant quite different things.

structure.title: Time Passes · A house with the family gone
structure.text: Woolf has given a dinner enough room for a dozen private anxieties. Now she gives years to an empty house almost in passing. Air creeps indoors, things come loose, and people have to come in and clean. Events that would take up chapters in a family history can fit inside a pair of brackets.

structure.title: The Lighthouse · Two things still to be done
structure.text: Years later, a boat sets out and Lily Briscoe stands at her easel again. The boat and the canvas give a morning two quite different destinations. Lily can shift her picture with a stroke of the brush, but she can no longer turn to the people she once watched and ask them what they meant.

people.name: Mrs Ramsay
people.role: Hostess, wife and mother of eight
people.text: She can spot a guest left out of a conversation and find exactly the words to draw him back in. She is equally quick to imagine whom a young woman ought to marry. Part of the pleasure of following her thoughts is seeing how readily a gift for understanding people can turn into making plans for them.

people.name: Mr Ramsay
people.text: He values an accurate forecast enough to disappoint a small boy over it. Alone with his own thoughts, he worries that other minds have gone further than his and that his work will be forgotten. The reader hears the fear beneath a demand for comfort before the person expected to supply it has had a chance to answer.

people.name: Lily Briscoe
people.text: The mother and child at the window become a difficulty about the placement of colour on Lily's canvas. Someone else can look at her picture and scarcely make them out. Lily has to find out whether she can trust the thing she sees enough to put it where she thinks it belongs.

context.title: Whose thought just entered the sentence?
context.text: A guest crosses a room, and a sentence about how disagreeable he is may belong to the person watching him. A few lines later the reader can be hearing what he thinks of the watcher. A change in tone, an unkind nickname or a sudden preoccupation with clothes can mark the crossing.

context.title: The dinner and the painting both take work
context.text: Mrs Ramsay wants to bring a tableful of people into conversation. Lily wants to bring separate patches of colour into a relation she can believe in. Each woman has to judge whether the pieces go together, and the book is sharply attentive to who thinks a woman capable of that judgment and what becomes of the thing she has made.

notice.text: Watch what Lily does with the salt cellar at dinner.
notice.why: A painter's problem has followed her to the table. She moves an ordinary object to remind herself of a change she wants to make to the picture. Even while the guests seem to share one occasion, Lily is also somewhere else, working.

passages.quote: She took up the salt cellar and put it down again

notice.text: Listen to the answers Mrs Ramsay gives her husband.
notice.why: He may appear to ask about a book or the weather. She has to work out when he wants agreement, praise or a declaration of love. The apparent simplicity of their exchanges depends on how much of that work she is willing to do silently.

notice.text: Notice the hands it takes to bring an empty house back.
notice.why: Wind and damp get whole passages in the middle section. Then Mrs McNab and others have to lift, scrub and fetch. A house that seems, from the family's point of view, to have waited patiently for them has an entirely different history in the hands of the people who kept it standing.

opening: A boy wants to visit a lighthouse, his mother says they might, and his father announces that the weather will be bad. The hurt lasts far longer than the exchange. Around them, guests talk, a painter struggles with her picture, and Mrs Ramsay works to make an evening hold together. Woolf follows the thoughts nobody quite manages to say, before years pass through the house and leave the survivors trying to recover what they scarcely knew they possessed.
